minor_characters.name: Adolph
minor_characters.appearances_summary: St. Clare’s self-styled valet/dandy in the New Orleans household; flits through parlor, kitchen, and sale scenes as comic foil and to be sold at auction later.
minor_characters.reason_removable: He is comic color and a class-contrast but has no effect on the plot beats or the arcs preserved in the synopsis.

minor_characters.name: Jane and Rosa
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Quadroon maids in Marie’s and Miss Ophelia’s orbit; appear in kitchen parodies, gossip, and as background in Eva’s rooms.
minor_characters.reason_removable: They provide local color and minor banter; removing them does not affect any required event or decision.

minor_characters.name: Mammy (Eva’s nurse)
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Old nurse who fusses over Marie and loves Eva; present at the lake villa and in New Orleans during Eva’s decline.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Her presence heightens sentiment but no plot turn depends on her.

minor_characters.name: Mr. Marks
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Tom Loker’s sly associate met at the tavern and in the river pursuit of Eliza.
minor_characters.reason_removable: Loker’s pursuit, wounding, and later change of heart can be shown without his sidekick; Marks adds banter but no plot hinge.

minor_characters.name: Mr. Skeggs
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Dealer who runs the New Orleans depot and primes slaves for auction.
minor_characters.reason_removable: He is a transactional facilitator with no lasting role in the story’s required arcs.

minor_characters.name: Henrique St. Clare
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Alfred St. Clare’s spirited son who visits briefly; flirtatious with Eva and cruel to his groom Dodo.
minor_characters.reason_removable: His episode is a didactic contrast that does not alter the St. Clare/Eva/Tom arc preserved in the synopsis.

minor_characters.name: Alfred St. Clare
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Augustine’s twin brother who visits with Henrique and debates politics and slavery.
minor_characters.reason_removable: He is a philosophical foil; nothing in the synopsis depends on his scenes.

minor_characters.name: Dodo
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Henrique’s mulatto groom boy, present only in the Henrique visit to illustrate petty master–slave cruelty.
minor_characters.reason_removable: He exists solely within the cuttable Henrique subplot and can be removed with it.

minor_characters.name: Aunt Dorcas
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Quaker nurse who tends Tom Loker during his convalescence and banters him out of swearing while he’s bedridden (Ch 038).
minor_characters.reason_removable: She is a one-scene caregiver whose name and personality can be elided without changing Loker’s Quaker-aided recovery already required by the synopsis.

minor_characters.name: Mrs. Smyth
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Respectable Canadian woman who poses as Harry’s 'aunty' and travels with George and Eliza on the lake packet to Amherstburg (Ch 038).
minor_characters.reason_removable: Her named role can be replaced by an unnamed helper or folded into the Quaker network without affecting the escape-to-Canada arc.

minor_characters.name: Marks
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A slave-catcher who briefly appears at the Sandusky wharf, conferring with the packet clerk as the fugitives board (Ch 038).
minor_characters.reason_removable: His cameo adds momentary tension but no plot turn, and the boat scene reads cleanly without identifying him.

minor_characters.name: Tompkins
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A neighboring planter used only as Legree’s cotton-wager foil in plantation talk (Ch 037).
minor_characters.reason_removable: He is a name-check for Legree’s bragging and can be cut without loss.

minor_characters.name: Captain Stuart
minor_characters.appearances_summary: In Cassy’s backstory, a kindly purchaser who frees and tries to recover her children (Ch 035).
minor_characters.reason_removable: He exists only inside the optional autobiography and drops out of the main action.

minor_characters.name: Butler
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Cassy’s abusive owner in her backstory who sells her children and provokes her attempted attack (Ch 035).
minor_characters.reason_removable: Another backstory figure whose details are not needed to understand Cassy’s despair and later stratagem.

minor_characters.name: Simmons
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Named only as the seller on Eliza’s bill of sale recalled aboard the steamer (Ch 043).
minor_characters.reason_removable: A paperwork name that can be omitted without changing the discovery that Eliza is Cassy’s child.

minor_characters.name: Lucy
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A sick mulatto field hand whose short weight triggers Tom’s aid and Legree’s order that Tom flog her (Ch 034).
minor_characters.reason_removable: Her specific name is unnecessary—the refusal-to-flog scene works with an unnamed, ailing woman.

subplots.name: Prue the bakery woman
subplots.reason_removable: Prue’s tragic vignette amplifies themes of cruelty but no main-character decision or synopsis beat depends on it.

subplots.name: Henrique’s visit and Dodo’s mistreatment
subplots.reason_removable: This visit is a moral contrast and does not change the St. Clare household arc or any later necessity.

subplots.name: Aunt Chloe hired out in Louisville to earn Tom’s redemption money
subplots.reason_removable: It humanizes Shelby’s people but does not affect Tom’s downstream sale, Legree’s purchase, or the synopsis-required resolutions.

subplots.name: Miss Ophelia’s housekeeping crusade and kitchen comedy
subplots.reason_removable: These scenes satirize northern neatness and teach Topsy slowly, but Topsy’s introduction and moral turn can stand without the housekeeping set-pieces.

subplots.name: Cassy’s full autobiography (the 'Quadroon’s Story')
subplots.reason_removable: A long embedded life history that can be drastically compressed to 'years of abuse, children sold' without changing her function as Legree’s victim and Tom’s later ally.

subplots.name: Legree’s cotton-wager rivalries
subplots.reason_removable: Talk of out-harvesting Tompkins and betting on crop yields colors Legree but doesn’t alter any plot decision.

subplots.name: Marks stalking the Sandusky boat
subplots.reason_removable: A brief cat-and-mouse beat that heightens suspense yet adds no new consequence once the fugitives cast off.

subplots.name: Ghost-legend embroidery after the garret ruse
subplots.reason_removable: An atmospheric extension of the 'haunting' that repeats the point of Legree’s superstition after the stratagem has already worked.

subplots.name: Emmeline’s boy-disguise makeover comedy
subplots.reason_removable: Light business around hair-cutting, caps and poses can be trimmed to a line that she travels safely in disguise.

digressions.topic: Author’s editorial asides on the ‘lawful trade’ and polite society’s tolerance of slave-catching
digressions.reason_removable: The polemic does not advance the plot; the auction and pursuit still read cleanly without narrator intrusions.

digressions.topic: St. Clare’s broad social theory—aristocracy vs. democracy, English vs. American labor
digressions.reason_removable: Philosophical framing of slavery can be trimmed without losing required character or event beats.

digressions.topic: Extended salons of argument (St. Clare, Marie, Miss Ophelia) about ‘systems’ and north–south morality
digressions.reason_removable: These essays-in-dialogue slow the story and can be tightened or cut without harming the synopsis arc.

digressions.topic: Narrator’s moral addresses around Prue, northern prejudice, and church-going hypocrisy
digressions.reason_removable: They are thematic digressions; the story’s needed events (Eva’s decline; Tom’s sale) proceed without them.

digressions.topic: Authorial aside comparing 'picking cotton isn’t hard work' to the Inquisition’s water-drop torture and the deadening monotony of forced labor.
digressions.reason_removable: It is a thematic lecture that can be cut or tightened without affecting the Legree-plantation setup.

digressions.topic: Apostrophe on 'Liberty'—national vs. individual freedom—with rhetorical questions to American readers.
digressions.reason_removable: A stirring essay that pauses the fugitives’ departure and can be abbreviated without narrative loss.

digressions.topic: Mini-essay that 'no one is so thoroughly superstitious as the godless man,' contrasting Christian order with dread of the spirit-land.
digressions.reason_removable: A homiletic gloss on Legree’s fear that reiterates a point already clear from action.

digressions.topic: Playful 'pneumatology' on why ghosts wear white sheets (with Shakespeare citation) and a general musing on souls and locked doors.
digressions.reason_removable: A witty aside that neither advances plot nor deepens character beyond the already-established haunting.

skippable_chapters.reason_removable: Miss Ophelia’s extended housekeeping battles and kitchen satire neither set up nor pay off any synopsis-required beat.
The Prue episode is a stand‑alone social vignette; its details don’t alter Eva’s illness, Tom’s fate, or the St. Clare arc the synopsis depends on.
Aunt Chloe’s Louisville hire-out plan is a side thread; Tom’s path to Legree and the Shelby ending in the synopsis do not rely on it.
Henrique’s visit is a didactic interlude; removing it leaves the Eva–St. Clare–Tom trajectory and New Orleans household arc intact.
Cassy’s extended backstory occupies most of the chapter and her crucial present-tense role (tending Tom, beginning to soften) can be conveyed in a few lines.
skippable_chapters.kernel: After Tom’s brutal whipping, Cassy secretly brings him water and dresses his wounds in the gin-house; hardened by years of sale and abuse and the loss of her children, she rages that God has forsaken them, but at Tom’s urging she reads of Christ’s forgiveness and, though despairing still, begins to be moved. She hints at a long, bitter history that has made her what she is.

skippable_chapters.reason_removable: It elaborates ghostly lore and Legree’s nightmares and then narrates, at length, the flight of Cassy and Emmeline and their chance boat-meeting, all of which the next chapter summarizes and uses without needing the full scene.
skippable_chapters.kernel: As ghost rumors spread, Cassy and Emmeline slip from the garret in disguise—Cassy as a Creole lady, Emmeline as her maid—reach the riverboats, and there encounter George Shelby and a French lady, Madame de Thoux, who reveals herself as George Harris’s sister; hearing names and papers, Cassy first suspects that Eliza may be her long-lost child. Legree’s terror intensifies, and that night the house is found open as two white figures vanish down the avenue.

force_keep_chapters.reason: Concluding Remarks carries Stowe's explicit source claims and moral synthesis; the book critic treats those themes as required coverage.
